title: Marguerite and the Letter
premise: In 1793, apprentice clockmaker Silas Pemberton is summoned to repair the observatory's failing master clock, a job that will make or break his master's workshop. At the door he finds a frightened child, Marguerite, left with a sealed letter and the instruction to forget her face — but the letter implicates a judge in a murder, and its author, a fugitive printer named Delacroix, is Silas's estranged father. As royalist agents close in on the workshop and the clock's gears hold a hidden cipher, Silas must choose between loyalty to the man who raised him and the truth that could save an innocent woman from the gallows. He finishes the clock, exposes the letter at the assizes, loses the workshop to fire, and gains a family: himself, Marguerite, and the father he thought he'd buried.
about_author: Rosalind Pemberton is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing provincial court records and horological ledgers from the 1790s. She writes historical fiction about ordinary people caught in the machinery of history, and lives near a decommissioned observatory she has never been allowed inside.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Silas Pemberton, POV. In his master Whitcombe's cramped workshop, Silas repairs a merchant's watch and reflects that history happens elsewhere, to other people. Whitcombe announces the observatory commission — their last chance at solvency. Beat: quiet ambition shadowed by dread of failure.

chapters.title: A Knock After Midnight
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. A hooded woman leaves a seven-year-old girl, Marguerite, on the doorstep with a sealed letter and the words 'forget my face.' Silas hides the child as boots pass in the street. Beat: fear crystallizing into reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: The Letter He Should Have Burned
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Alone, he breaks the seal: the letter names Judge Harrow as the man who murdered a printer's wife, and begs whoever reads it to carry it to the assizes. The handwriting is unmistakably his father's — dead these ten years. Beat: vertigo; his ordered world cracks.

chapters.title: The Observatory Clock
chapters.summary: Silas, POV, with Marguerite hidden in the workshop. He begins work on the master clock's stripped escapement while memorizing the letter against discovery. The astronomer Mr. Quill notices his distraction. Beat: divided attention, first ticking of the deadline.

chapters.title: What the Girl Remembers
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV. The child describes the night her mother was taken: a judge's carriage, a printed page used to wrap bread. She doesn't know the letter exists. Beat: innocence carrying terrible testimony; Silas realizes she is evidence.

chapters.title: Harrow Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Judge Harrow arrives for the assizes and visits the observatory, admiring the clock, lingering on Silas's hands. A royalist agent, Cade, follows him. Beat: the predator enters the story politely.

chapters.title: Whitcombe's Debt
chapters.summary: Whitcombe, POV. Flashback chapter: how Whitcombe took in young Silas after Delacroix fled a printing sedition charge, and what he sacrificed. He suspects the girl's presence and says nothing. Beat: love expressed as silence; loyalty established.

chapters.title: The Cipher in the Escapement
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Cleaning the clock's plates, Silas finds punched holes matching the letter's pinpricks — his father hid the true names in the mechanism years ago. The letter alone can be dismissed; the clock cannot. Beat: revelation; the machine becomes a witness.

chapters.title: Cade Searches the Workshop
chapters.summary: Silas and Marguerite, alternating. Cade arrives with a warrant 'for seditious print,' turning over benches while Marguerite hides in the clock case itself. He leaves unconvinced. Beat: claustrophobic terror; the noose tightens.

chapters.title: The Man Who Was Dead
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Following the letter's second instruction, Silas finds his father alive under a new name, keeping a country bindery. Delacroix refuses to testify: exposure means the gallows for him and ruin for Silas. Beat: betrayal and recognition entangled.

chapters.title: An Innocent Woman in the Cells
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV. Through Quill's kindness the children learn that Mrs. Aubry, the printer's widow's friend, stands trial for the murder in three days. Marguerite insists they act; Silas hesitates. Beat: conscience sharpened by a child's clarity.

chapters.title: Loyalty Weighs Its Price
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Whitcombe begs him to finish the clock and burn the letter — the workshop survives only if they stay invisible. Silas nearly agrees. Beat: the theme made explicit; lowest moral point before resolve.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Decided
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV. The child slips out alone to deliver a copied fragment of the letter to Mrs. Aubry's advocate, nearly taken by Cade's men. Silas retrieves her in the rain. Beat: courage shaming caution; partnership formed.

chapters.title: The Advocate's Bargain
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Advocate Lisle will use the letter only if Silas testifies and produces the clock's cipher as corroboration — meaning the observatory commission becomes evidence, and Whitcombe's livelihood hangs on the trial's outcome. Beat: stakes braided together.

chapters.title: Night Work
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Racing the assizes, Silas rebuilds the escapement so the cipher can be read without destroying the clock, working by candle while Cade watches the street. Delacroix sends a key part anonymously. Beat: craftsmanship as resistance; hope kindled.

chapters.title: The First Day of Trial
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Mrs. Aubry's trial opens; Harrow presides over the case that would implicate him. Lisle's opening is deflected; the letter is challenged as forgery. Beat: despair; the law protecting itself.

chapters.title: The Clock Speaks
chapters.summary: Silas, POV, climax part one. Against Whitcombe's plea, Silas brings the court to the observatory and demonstrates the punched-plate cipher before judge, jury, and assembled town. The names align exactly with the letter. Beat: public truth; the room turns.

chapters.title: Harrow's Fall and Cade's Fire
chapters.summary: Alternating Silas and Marguerite. Harrow orders Silas seized; the crowd resists. Retreating, Cade fires the workshop. Whitcombe goes in for the finished regulator and is burned saving it. Beat: climax; victory purchased with loss.

chapters.title: Ashes and Accounts
chapters.summary: Whitcombe, POV. The workshop is rubble; Harrow flees and is taken at the coast. Whitcombe reckons what remains: the saved regulator, the boy, the girl. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance; justice outside the law acknowledged.

chapters.title: Delacroix Stands Up
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. His father surrenders voluntarily, choosing testimony over flight, and is spared for turning crown's evidence. Father and son speak plainly for the first time. Beat: identity resolved; the dead name laid down.

chapters.title: The Master Clock Runs
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. The observatory clock strikes the hour flawlessly; Quill offers Silas the keeper's post. Marguerite asks if she may stop being forgotten. Beat: restoration; time running toward them now instead of out.

chapters.title: Marguerite and the Letter
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV, coda. A year later, in the rebuilt workshop bearing both names — Pemberton & Pemberton — she keeps the letter framed beside the bench, no longer evidence but memory. Silas teaches her the escapement. Beat: peace earned; the face remembered after all.
